title: Sleep first
hook: lost sleep worsens mood and attention, and regular timing helps

segments.voice: Yesterday: gratitude, honestly. Your line was small still counts. Did you pick your one day this week for five things, lightly? Day three hundred twenty.

It's 11:40 at night. You're tired, properly tired. And you're watching one more episode. Or answering one more message. Or lying in bed scrolling past things you won't remember tomorrow. Some people call it revenge bedtime procrastination: the day belonged to everyone else, so you steal the night back for yourself, and pay for it in the morning. Here's an uncomfortable truth for anyone on a path like this one. Every practice we've learned this year, the breathing, the noticing, the kindness, the patience, gets harder when you're short on sleep. Before meditation, before gratitude, before any of it: sleep first.
screen: `11:40, ONE MORE EPISODE.` → `STEALING THE NIGHT BACK.` → `BEFORE ANY OF IT: SLEEP.`

segments.voice: First, mood. Researchers have kept volunteers awake, or cut their sleep short for a few nights, and measured what happens. One review of many such studies found that mood took an even bigger hit than thinking or physical skills. After short sleep, people tend to feel more irritable, more anxious, and quicker to see things as threats. The patience you practiced all year is running on a low battery. Second, attention. Sleep-deprived people miss more on simple attention tasks, and they're often poor judges of how impaired they are. They feel almost fine. Third, timing, which may be the most overlooked part. Your body keeps a daily clock. Studies of students and adults have linked irregular sleep, going to bed at very different times from night to night, to worse mood and poorer grades, even when total hours were similar. Many sleep experts suggest adults aim for seven hours or more, at a roughly steady time. A caution: the field has had overblown claims too, and not everyone needs exactly the same amount. The solid part is plain: short and scattered sleep makes most things harder. Fourth, the old wisdom. Monasteries and religious communities have long closed the day with night prayers and a time of quiet. A Psalm in the King James words says "It is vain for you to rise up early, to sit up late, to eat the bread of sorrows: for so he giveth his beloved sleep." Whatever you believe about the giver, the psalmist saw sleep as a gift, not as a weakness to push through. Sleep isn't the opposite of practice. It's the ground practice stands on.
screen: `SHORT SLEEP HITS MOOD HARDEST.` · `ATTENTION SLIPS, AND WE DON'T NOTICE.` · `A STEADY TIME HELPS.` · `HE GIVETH HIS BELOVED SLEEP.` · then, large: `SLEEP FIRST.`

segments.voice: Use these two minutes to plan tonight. What time do you want to be asleep? Count back half an hour. That's when screens go down, lights go low. Picture yourself there tonight: what will you be doing, where will the phone be? Maybe charging outside the bedroom. Now just breathe slowly, the way you will when your head hits the pillow, six a minute if you like. The bell holds the time.
Sleep first. Short sleep hits mood and attention, and a steady bedtime helps. The ground every other practice stands on. Today's word.
Your line: sleep first. Keep your bedtime tonight. When the one-more-episode voice starts, say to it, kindly: sleep first. Day three hundred twenty.

howItsDone: Many people protect a regular bedtime with a short wind-down, lights low and screens away; many religious communities close the day with night prayers and quiet.
